query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys (HEAs), service-relevant cyclic thermal–mechanical loading triggers stress-assisted segregation of slower‐diffusing elements to the grain boundaries, leading to the nucleation of nanoscale brittle intergranular phases. This process, arising from the intrinsic chemistry and local ordering of HEAs, produces a distinct toughness degradation mechanism compared to conventional alloys that degrade primarily via grain-boundary segregation and coarse intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., a CrMnFeCoNi-type alloy) with a homogeneous distribution of elements and undisturbed grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA and a conventional alloy (with similar baseline grain size and toughness) to controlled cyclic mechanical loading combined with thermal aging at service-relevant temperatures to accelerate diffusion and stress-assisted segregation.
generation.conditions: Identical cyclic fatigue and thermal aging protocols are applied to both the HEA and a conventional alloy under laboratory-simulated service conditions. Measurements are carried out before, during, and after intervention, focusing on grain-boundary chemistry and toughness metrics.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary compositional changes leading to the formation of nanoscale brittle precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic loading and thermal aging, certain slower-diffusing elements in the HEA partition to the grain boundaries. This localized segregation promotes the nucleation of fine brittle phases which reduce the ductility and overall toughness of the alloy, in contrast to the precipitation behavior observed in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Post-intervention, the HEA will exhibit detectable nanoscale brittle precipitates along grain boundaries (observed via TEM and atom probe analysis) along with a measurable reduction in toughness (e.g., lower impact energy in Charpy tests) relative to its initial state and differing mechanistically from conventional alloys under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous, high-toughness single-phase microstructure with no significant grain-boundary segregation or brittle precipitation prior to loading and aging.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under service-relevant conditions featuring moderate thermal aging (e.g., temperatures that enhance element mobility without triggering full phase transformations) combined with cyclic mechanical stress. The mechanism may not be significant in temperature regimes or loading conditions where diffusion is negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative significance of toughness reduction and the kinetics of elemental segregation in different HEA compositions remain uncertain and may vary with subtle differences in alloying elements and service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of a compositionally complex HEA and one of a comparable conventional alloy. Expose both sets to identical cyclic mechanical loading and thermal aging treatments designed to simulate service conditions. Use TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) to inspect grain-boundary regions for nanoscale brittle precipitates, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., Charpy impact tests) to evaluate toughness before and after treatment.
measurements: Grain-boundary elemental composition via atom probe tomography
Nanostructural analysis of precipitates via transmission electron microscopy
Mechanical toughness measurements (impact energy, crack growth resistance)
In-situ fatigue crack propagation via scanning electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples do not show evidence of stress-assisted grain-boundary segregation and formation of nanoscale brittle phases, or if the toughness degradation is similar in magnitude and mechanism to that of the conventional alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
